title: Relational, document or graph? Choosing the shape
objectives: Explain what the relational, document and graph models each make cheap and expensive, and pick one from an application's read and write patterns
Choose embedding or referencing for a MongoDB document from what's read together, what changes on its own, and what grows without bound
Use PostgreSQL `jsonb` correctly — `->` vs `->>`, casts, `@>` with a GIN index, expression indexes — and name what it gives up
Answer a variable-depth relationship question with a recursive CTE, and say when a graph database earns its place

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: JSON Types (jsonb, containment, GIN indexing)
PostgreSQL 18 docs: JSON Functions and Operators
PostgreSQL 18 docs: WITH Queries (recursive, SEARCH, CYCLE)
Neo4j docs: What is a graph database

questions.prompt: A billing system: customers, subscriptions, invoices, payments. Finance asks new questions weekly ("revenue by plan by region, excluding refunds"), and an invoice must never point at a customer that doesn't exist. Which model fits best?

options.text: Relational — integrity rules and ad-hoc queries across entities are exactly what it's built for
Document — embed invoices and payments inside each customer document
Graph — customers, invoices and payments are all connected
Any of them; the model doesn't affect which queries are easy

questions.explanation: Cross-cutting questions nobody planned for, plus referential integrity, are the relational model's home ground: each fact lives once, foreign keys enforce the links, and any new report is just a query. Embedding everything in customer documents makes per-customer reads cheap and every cross-customer report a scan of every document. "It's connected" describes all data; a graph database pays off for deep traversals, not for sums and filters.

questions.prompt: A page builder stores each page as a tree of content blocks whose fields vary by block type. Pages are always loaded and saved whole; nobody queries across pages by block field. What fits?

options.text: A document per page — in a document store, or a `jsonb` column on a `pages` table
A table per block type, joined back together on every page load
A graph database, since blocks nest inside blocks
One `attributes(page_id, block_id, key, value)` table for every field

questions.explanation: The page is an aggregate: read together, written together, varying shape, no cross-page queries — the case MongoDB's guide sums up as "data that's accessed together should be stored together". A `jsonb` column gives the same shape inside PostgreSQL, next to relational data that needs integrity. A table per block type means many joins to rebuild what's always used whole; nesting isn't a reason for a graph database when you never traverse it.

questions.prompt: In MongoDB, should an order's line items be embedded in the order document or stored in their own collection?

options.text: Embed — they're only meaningful inside the order, read with it, and changed with it in one atomic write
Reference — related data should always live in its own collection
Both, kept in sync by the application
Neither — line items need a graph store

questions.explanation: MongoDB's embedding guidance: "contains" and one-to-many relationships where the children are viewed in the context of the parent. An order's items are read with it and change with it, and a single-document write is atomic. Storing them twice and syncing them recreates the update anomaly embedding was meant to avoid.

questions.prompt: Orders embed a copy of the customer's current email and loyalty tier "for fast display". Customers change both regularly. What's the better design?

options.text: Store `customerId` on the order and keep the email and tier in the customer document — frequently changing data shouldn't be copied
Keep the copies and update every order whenever the customer changes
Keep the copies and wrap each customer update in a multi-document transaction
Embed the orders inside the customer document instead

questions.explanation: MongoDB's referencing guidance lists exactly this: embedding that duplicates data that frequently changes, without enough read benefit to justify it. These copies aren't snapshots ("the email at time of order") — they're meant to be current, so every change becomes a fan-out update. A transaction makes that fan-out atomic but not cheap. Embedding orders in the customer grows the customer document without bound.

questions.prompt: A post document embeds an array of every comment. A post goes viral. What limit is the design heading for?

options.text: MongoDB's maximum document size (documents must be smaller than 16 MiB) — unbounded children belong in their own collection
None — arrays in MongoDB grow without limit
The 64-index limit per collection
Writes to it will need multi-document transactions

questions.explanation: An embedded array that grows with activity has no natural ceiling, but documents do: smaller than 16 MiB. Comments are also often queried on their own (latest across the site, by author), another reason MongoDB's guide gives for referencing. Adding a comment is still a single-document write, so transactions aren't the issue.

questions.prompt: `products.attrs` has `CREATE INDEX … USING GIN (attrs)`, yet `WHERE (attrs->>'qty')::int < 5` is a sequential scan on PostgreSQL 18. Why, and the fix?

options.text: A GIN index on the column serves containment and key-exists operators (`@>`, `?`), not a comparison on an extracted, cast value — add an expression index on `((attrs->>'qty')::int)`
Statistics are stale; `ANALYZE` will make it use the GIN index
Rebuild the GIN index with `jsonb_path_ops`
Switch the column to `json`, which indexes every key

questions.explanation: The GIN index stores the document's keys and values for `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&` (and jsonpath matching). `(attrs->>'qty')::int < 5` is a different expression with a different operator, so the index can't answer it — the same "index the expression you query" rule as `lower(email)`. `jsonb_path_ops` supports fewer operators, not more, and `json` is slower to query, not better indexed.

questions.prompt: `attrs->>'supplier_id'` must always name a real supplier. What does PostgreSQL 18 let you do?

options.text: Promote it: a `STORED` generated column `(attrs->>'supplier_id')::bigint` with `REFERENCES suppliers (id)`, or a plain column
Declare `FOREIGN KEY ((attrs->>'supplier_id')) REFERENCES suppliers (id)` directly
A virtual generated column with `REFERENCES`, since virtual is the default in PostgreSQL 18
A GIN index on `attrs` enforces it

questions.explanation: A foreign key needs real columns — `FOREIGN KEY ((expression))` is a syntax error. A stored generated column derives the value from the JSON and can carry the foreign key, so writers still send one document. A virtual generated column can't: PostgreSQL 18 rejects it with "foreign key constraints on virtual generated columns are not supported". Indexes speed lookups; they don't enforce references.

questions.prompt: Two features: (a) "show everyone in my reporting line" on an org chart of 5,000 people; (b) a product whose core is real-time recommendations from paths 3–4 hops deep across hundreds of millions of follow edges. What fits each?

options.text: (a) a recursive CTE in PostgreSQL; (b) a strong case for a graph database
A graph database for both — any hierarchy is a graph
Recursive CTEs for both — SQL can always do it fast enough
Plain joins for both, one join per level

questions.explanation: A tree of 5,000 rows is a few rounds of index lookups in a recursive CTE — no second system needed. Deep traversals over a huge, densely connected graph, where traversal *is* the product, are what graph databases are built for: the paths multiply by the fan-out at every hop in any system, but a graph store follows stored relationships instead of paying an index lookup and a join per hop. (a) has no fixed depth, so plain joins can't express it; (b) is bounded at 3–4 hops, but 3–4 self-joins over hundreds of millions of edges, on every request, is exactly the expensive part.

prompts.prompt: Compare a JSON field with a text literal.
prompts.code: SELECT id FROM products WHERE attrs___'color' = 'red';
prompts.explanation: `->>` extracts the value as `text`, so it compares with `'red'`. `->` returns `jsonb`, and `'red'` isn't valid JSON — that version fails with "invalid input syntax for type json".

prompts.prompt: Index the whole document, then query it with the operator that index serves.
code: CREATE INDEX products_attrs_gin ON products USING ___ (attrs);
SELECT id FROM products WHERE attrs ___ '{"color": "red"}';
prompts.explanation: GIN is the inverted index for values with many components; its default `jsonb` operator class serves `@>` (contains) and the key-exists operators. `@>` matches any document that *has* the pair, whatever else it holds.

prompts.prompt: Index and query a numeric key so it compares as a number, not as text.
prompts.explanation: The index must be on the same expression the query uses, cast included. Without the cast, `attrs->>'qty'` is text, where `'10' < '5'` is true.

prompts.prompt: Everyone below employee 1 in the org chart, at any depth.
code: SELECT id, name FROM employees WHERE manager_id = 1
SELECT e.id, e.name FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
prompts.explanation: `WITH RECURSIVE` lets the second term refer to the CTE itself; it re-runs against the previous round's rows until a round adds nothing. In a tree there are no cycles, so `UNION ALL` (no de-duplication) is safe and cheaper. In a graph with cycles, use the `CYCLE` clause (PostgreSQL 14+) or a depth bound.

code: SELECT attrs->>'qty' FROM products WHERE attrs->>'qty' > '9';
snippets.question: Which rows come back?
snippets.explanation: `->>` returns text, and text compares character by character: `'10'` and `'100'` start with `'1'`, which sorts before `'9'`, and `'9' > '9'` is false. Cast first — `(attrs->>'qty')::int > 9` returns 10 and 100.

snippets.code: SELECT id FROM products WHERE attrs->'color' = 'red';
snippets.question: What happens?
snippets.answer: ERROR: invalid input syntax for type json
acceptable: invalid input syntax for type json
snippets.explanation: `->` returns `jsonb`, so PostgreSQL reads the literal `'red'` as `jsonb` too — and a bare `red` isn't valid JSON (a JSON string needs quotes: `'"red"'`). Use `->>` to compare as text, or `@>` with a JSON object.

snippets.question: What text comes back?
snippets.explanation: `jsonb` doesn't keep duplicate keys (the last value wins) or the input's key order. `json` would return the input text exactly, duplicates and all. If key order or duplicates carry meaning, `jsonb` will lose it.

code: SELECT followee AS person FROM follows WHERE follower = 1
SELECT f.followee FROM follows f JOIN reach r ON f.follower = r.person
snippets.question: What does it return — and what if `UNION ALL` becomes `UNION`?
snippets.answer: It never finishes (1→2→3→1 loops forever); with UNION it returns 5 — persons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
snippets.explanation: With `UNION ALL` every round re-adds the rows reached through the cycle, so the working table never empties (on a test server it ran until `statement_timeout` cancelled it). `UNION` discards rows that duplicate any earlier result, so once 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 are found a round adds nothing and it stops. Once you track depth or paths, rows stop being duplicates — then you need a depth bound or the `CYCLE` clause.
